title: Attack and defend: SYN floods and DDoS
blurb: See how a SYN flood exhausts a server, then cap half-open connections on the ASA and plan upstream DDoS mitigation.
scenario: The public web server at **172.16.1.10** stops answering. The ASA shows tens of thousands of half-open connections from spoofed addresses. Work out what's happening, limit it on the ASA, and decide what to do when the flood is bigger than your Internet link.
topology: Internet ── ISP ── ASA (outside) ── DMZ web server 172.16.1.10
objectives: Explain how a SYN flood exhausts resources
Set connection limits with the Modular Policy Framework
Choose the right layer for a volumetric attack

steps.title: How the flood works
steps.learn: A TCP connection needs three packets: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. A server that gets a SYN reserves memory and waits for the ACK. In a **SYN flood**, the attacker sends huge numbers of SYNs from spoofed addresses and never sends the ACK. The server's table of **embryonic (half-open)** connections fills up, and real users can't connect.
steps.question: What resource does a SYN flood use up?

options.text: The table of half-open connections waiting for the final ACK

options.why: Nothing is written to disk. The pressure is on connection state in memory.
The flood never gets past the TCP handshake, so TLS isn't reached.

steps.title: Spot the indicators
steps.learn: Floods look different from a busy day. Watch for a jump in **embryonic connections**, many sources that each send only a SYN, and syslog messages about connection limits.
steps.task: Mark each observation as a flood indicator or not.

fields.label: Thousands of source IPs, each sending one SYN and nothing else
%ASA-6-302013 Built inbound TCP connection, followed by a teardown with 30 KB of data
%ASA-4-733100 Object drop rate exceeded for SYN attack

steps.title: Match the web traffic
steps.learn: On the ASA, connection limits use the **Modular Policy Framework**: an ACL picks the traffic, a **class map** matches the ACL, and a **policy map** sets the action.
steps.task: Create ACL **WEB-SRV** permitting TCP from any to host **172.16.1.10** on **www**. Create class map **WEB-CLASS** that matches it.
steps.hint: `access-list WEB-SRV extended permit tcp any host 172.16.1.10 eq www`, `class-map WEB-CLASS`, `match access-list WEB-SRV`.

commands.cmd: access-list WEB-SRV extended permit tcp any host 172.16.1.10 eq www

steps.title: Cap half-open connections
steps.learn: `set connection` limits total connections (**conn-max**), half-open connections (**embryonic-conn-max**) and half-open connections per client. When the embryonic limit is reached, the ASA uses **TCP Intercept**: it answers SYNs itself with SYN cookies and only opens a connection to the server once the client completes the handshake. Spoofed SYNs never reach the server.
steps.task: Create policy map **OUTSIDE-POLICY**. For class **WEB-CLASS**, allow **5000** connections, **500** embryonic connections, and **25** embryonic connections per client. Apply the policy to the **outside** interface.
steps.hint: `policy-map OUTSIDE-POLICY`, `class WEB-CLASS`, `set connection conn-max 5000 embryonic-conn-max 500 per-client-embryonic-max 25`, then `service-policy OUTSIDE-POLICY interface outside`.

commands.note: An interface policy overrides the global policy for traffic on that interface.

steps.title: Verify
steps.task: Show the service policy statistics for the outside interface.

commands.output:
Interface outside:
  Service-policy: OUTSIDE-POLICY
    Class-map: WEB-CLASS
      Set connection policy: conn-max 5000 embryonic-conn-max 500 per-client-embryonic-max 25
        current embryonic conns 500, drop 38412
      Set connection advanced-options: tcp-intercept
        current conns 212, drop 0
commands.note: The ASA holds embryonic connections at 500 and drops the rest. Real users still get through.

steps.title: When the pipe is full
steps.learn: Firewall limits protect the server, but they can't help when a **volumetric** flood fills your Internet link before traffic reaches the ASA. That has to be stopped upstream. **RTBH (remotely triggered black hole)** routing has the ISP drop all traffic to the attacked address, which stops the flood but also takes that address offline. A **cloud scrubbing service** reroutes your traffic, filters out the attack, and sends clean traffic back.
steps.task: Pick the best response for each situation.

fields.label: 50,000 SYNs per second; the link is fine but the server struggles
options: ASA connection limits and TCP Intercept
fields.answer: ASA connection limits and TCP Intercept

fields.label: 40 Gbps flood at an unused test address; the link is saturated
options: ASA connection limits and TCP Intercept

fields.label: 40 Gbps flood at the main web site, which must stay online
options: ASA connection limits and TCP Intercept

summary: How SYN floods fill the half-open table, flood indicators in ASA logs, MPF connection limits with TCP Intercept, and when to use RTBH or cloud scrubbing for volumetric attacks.
